captions.linkedin:
When my 10‑year‑old demanded a tech‑free hour, the whole family discovered how quickly silence can turn into conversation.

We put every device in the living‑room basket, set a timer on the tablet, and let the hour run its course.

The kids put their phones away without any reminder from me.

By dinner, the chatter shifted from “Did you see that video?” to “What was the best part of your day?”

Pew Research shows families with clear screen limits enjoy 30 % more face‑to‑face interaction.

Seeing my kids choose the limit themselves felt like a small but powerful step toward the digital habits we want to nurture.

captions.linkedin:
I still remember the night we finally sat down at the kitchen table, the kids’ phones buzzing on the counter, and I said, “I’m scared you might see something that hurts you.” The words felt clumsy at first, but the moment we stopped pretending the internet was a harmless playground, the conversation opened up. My oldest, who was already scrolling through memes, asked why I cared, and I answered with a simple fact: a recent Pew Research study found that 70 % of teens have encountered cyberbullying at least once. That number made the abstract worry concrete, and the kids’ eyes widened.

We talked about the kinds of messages they get, the ads that pop up while they watch videos, and the ways a stranger can slip into a group chat. I didn’t lecture; I shared a story from my own teenage years, when a friend’s profile was hacked and the fallout lasted weeks. The kids laughed at my outdated hairdo but listened when I described how that breach made the family feel helpless. Then we asked each other three questions: What do you enjoy online? What makes you uncomfortable? Who would you call if something went wrong? Those questions turned the talk from “I’m worried about you” to “Let’s figure this out together.”

The change was immediate. The next day, my daughter showed me a new privacy setting she’d found, and my son asked me to help him block a game that kept sending push notifications at night. By framing safety as a shared project, the fear faded and curiosity took its place. We still have those talks, especially after bedtime when the house quiets down and the glow of screens is the only light.

What was the conversation that changed everything for your family?
